title: Debugging Failed Steps
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of debugging failed steps and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to debugging failed steps.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on debugging failed steps. Find the first failed step, inspect its exit code and stderr, reproduce the command where possible, and distinguish application errors from runner/infrastructure failures. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Debugging Failed Steps matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Find the first failed step, inspect its exit code and stderr, reproduce the command where possible, and distinguish application errors from runner/infrastructure failures. Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Find the first failed step, inspect its exit code and stderr, reproduce the command where possible, and distinguish application errors from runner/infrastructure failures. Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Finding the first failing step
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Interpreting shell exit codes
items.text: For interpreting shell exit codes, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Investigating missing files
items.text: For investigating missing files, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Checking environment values
items.text: Use a GitHub Environment for deployment-specific secrets, variables, branch restrictions, and reviewer gates. Do not treat an environment name alone as proof that approval rules are configured.

items.title: Diagnosing dependency installation errors
items.text: Declare job dependencies with `needs` and read prerequisite results or outputs through `needs.<job>`. Separate jobs do not share a runner workspace automatically.

items.title: Separating command failures from runner failures
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

content_blocks.code:
steps:
  - name: Record a sanitized diagnostic
    if: ${{ failure() }}
    run: echo "A prior step failed; inspect its exit code and sanitized logs" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
content_blocks.expected_output: When a prior step fails, the summary adds a reminder to inspect logs without reproducing environment values or secrets.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to debugging failed steps. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain debugging failed steps, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Turn run status, logs, and diagnostic data into a systematic troubleshooting process.

content.task: Apply debugging failed steps to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Find the first failed step, inspect its exit code and stderr, reproduce the command where possible, and distinguish application errors from runner/infrastructure failures.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Find the first failed step, inspect its exit code and stderr, reproduce the command where possible, and distinguish application errors from runner/infrastructure failures. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Find the first failed step, inspect its exit code and stderr, reproduce the command where possible, and distinguish application errors from runner/infrastructure failures.

Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
